name: Clobetasol propionate

lead: Clobetasol propionate is the strongest class of topical corticosteroid, prescribed for psoriasis, eczema, lichen conditions and similar. It also appears as a hidden ingredient in illicit skin-lightening creams, where skin paling in the treated area is a side effect of its action.

It activates glucocorticoid receptors in the skin, dampening inflammation and suppressing pigment. The FDA has not approved it for lightening, and products containing it are sold internationally and online, sometimes at higher strength than prescription versions. A 2016 study cited in the sources ranks it with mercury and hydroquinone among the most toxic and most-used lightening agents. No trials have tested it for lightening.

paras: In prescription use it is a short-course cream or ointment applied to affected skin. In lightening products it is used undeclared inside creams, so people may apply it for long periods without knowing.

Reported effects include skin thinning, bruising, visible capillaries, stretch marks, acne, raised blood pressure and blood sugar, and adrenal suppression; Cushing's syndrome has been reported. The US label limits use to two weeks and 50 g per week, and it is prescription-only.

angle.text: Clobetasol is a prescription steroid for psoriasis and eczema that appears as a hidden ingredient in illicit lightening creams, where it suppresses pigment and paler skin follows. Use for lightening is off-label and unstudied, and its documented skin harms are significant.

lead: Clobetasol propionate is a super-high-potency topical corticosteroid, the top group in the seven-class US potency ranking.[1][2] It is prescribed for corticosteroid-responsive skin conditions such as psoriasis, eczema, contact dermatitis, lichen sclerosus and lichen planus, and as a treatment for cutaneous graft-versus-host disease.[1][2]

Its appearance role is through the skin conditions it treats. Calming inflammation in psoriasis plaques, eczema, lichen planus and patchy hair loss from alopecia areata makes skin and scalp look clearer, and it is one of the topical options studied in vitiligo.[2][3][4][5] A 1975 trial found it more effective than betamethasone valerate in psoriasis, and shampoo, foam, spray and ointment forms have each been trialled for the scalp and body.[6][7][8]

The drug also turns up as an undeclared or openly sold ingredient in skin-lightening creams. Wikipedia reports that the FDA has not approved it for that purpose and that products containing it are sold internationally and online, in some cases at higher concentrations than prescription products allow.[2] A survey-and-product study in Somaliland found that 12 of 56 locally purchased lightening products contained clobetasol, and a 2012 clinical letter describes a patient who developed adrenal suppression after using clobetasol-containing creams.[9][10] No clinical trial has tested it as a lightening treatment.

The US label restricts use to short courses and a maximum weekly amount because the drug can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.[1] Online communities also discuss clobetasol in connection with topical steroid withdrawal, a reported pattern of redness and burning after long-term topical steroid use.[11]

paras: Clobetasol is used for inflammatory skin and scalp conditions, where its appearance effect is visible clearing of plaques, redness and scale. It is also reported in lightening products outside approved use.

The US label describes it as indicated for relief of the inflammatory and itching manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses.[1] Wikipedia lists eczema, contact dermatitis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis (including scalp and plaque), lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, alopecia areata, mycosis fungoides and cutaneous graft-versus-host disease, in cream, foam, gel, solution, ointment and shampoo forms, and describes it as first-line for acute and chronic skin graft-versus-host disease.[2]
Grokipedia's account adds that it is not indicated for rosacea, perioral dermatitis, acne or primary skin infections.[12]

For people with visible skin disease, clobetasol is a route to clearer-looking skin: scalp psoriasis plaques flake less, lichen planus and eczema patches calm, and alopecia areata patches are among the conditions where reviews list topical clobetasol as an established option.[3][13][5] In childhood vitiligo, a double-blind randomised trial compared 0.05 percent clobetasol with 0.1 percent tacrolimus for repigmentation.[4]

Separately, Wikipedia reports that the drug is used for skin whitening, describes this as controversial, and notes that lightening creams containing it are found in some New York City beauty-supply stores and online.[2]

Clobetasol propionate is a synthetic glucocorticoid ester (ATC code D07AD01) believed to act by activating steroid receptors.[2] Grokipedia's account describes binding to glucocorticoid receptors in skin cells, repression of inflammatory signalling such as NF-kappa B, and vasoconstrictive effects that reduce redness and swelling.[12]

Topical corticosteroids are ranked in seven US potency classes, and clobetasol sits in the top, super-high-potency group, so it is typically reserved for short courses and for thick or stubborn plaques.[2] Because the drug is absorbed through the skin, the label warns that enough exposure can suppress the body's own steroid axis.[1] The Grokipedia account notes that absorption rises with inflamed, damaged or occluded skin and with large treated areas.[12]

Wikipedia reports that it was patented in 1968 and entered medical use in 1978 and is available as a generic; in 2023 it was the 129th most commonly prescribed medicine in the US, with more than 4 million prescriptions.[2]

Brand names include Clobex, Temovate, Dermovate, Olux and Impoyz, and the drug is sold as a generic in many forms from shampoo to foam.[2] Spray, foam and ointment versions have been compared in registered trials in plaque psoriasis, and an ophthalmic nanoemulsion was trialled after cataract surgery.[8][14]

A 1975 double-blind trial in 34 patients with psoriasis vulgaris found clobetasol propionate cream more effective than betamethasone valerate cream over two weeks, and 14 of 16 patients who had not responded to betamethasone valerate ointment improved quickly after switching.[6] A randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial examined clobetasol 0.05% for oral lichen planus.[15] Registered trials include clobetasol shampoo maintenance in scalp psoriasis (288 participants), spray versus foam and ointment comparisons in psoriasis, and an ophthalmic nanoemulsion after cataract surgery.[7][8][14]

A systematic review of 55 articles on oral lichen planus proposed an algorithm that puts topical clobetasol propionate at 0.025 to 0.05 percent as the first therapeutic option, followed by tacrolimus or pimecrolimus.[3] A double-blind randomised trial in childhood vitiligo compared 0.1 percent tacrolimus with 0.05 percent clobetasol, and reviews of scalp psoriasis and alopecia areata list topical clobetasol among established topical treatments.[4][13][5]
No studies found of clobetasol as a skin-lightening treatment. Observational work in that area consists of surveys, product analyses and case reports of harms.[9][10]

In label trials, the most frequent adverse events were burning, irritation and itching in about 0.5% of treated patients; less frequent reactions included stinging, cracking, redness, folliculitis, skin atrophy and telangiectasia, and Cushing's syndrome has been reported in infants and adults.[1] Wikipedia adds cellulitis, adrenal suppression and allergic reactions among serious effects.[2] A 1989 case report describes clobetasol-induced milia.

The label advises against treatment beyond two consecutive weeks and against exceeding 50 g a week because of the potential to suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.[1] Corticosteroids have been teratogenic in animals at relatively low systemic doses, clobetasol has not been tested for teratogenicity topically, and it is absorbed through the skin.[1]

Topical steroid withdrawal, also called red burning skin syndrome, is described as a pattern of redness, burning, itching and sometimes peeling that appears within weeks of stopping topical steroids used for two weeks or longer; reported named signs include the headlight sign and red sleeve.[11] It was first described in 1979, a systematic review appeared in 2016, and overall prevalence is unknown; one indirect estimate from a Japanese survey suggested about 12 percent of adults with atopic dermatitis treated with topical corticosteroids might be affected.[11] Wikipedia says thousands of people gather in online communities for mutual support, and that researchers have debated study design and biomarkers.[11] The condition can be hard to tell apart from the original skin disease.[11]

Skin-lightening products that contain clobetasol are reported on Wikipedia in some beauty-supply stores and online, sometimes at concentrations above those allowed in prescription products, and the FDA has not approved the drug for lightening.[2] Reported effects include skin thinning, easy bruising, visible capillaries, acne, stretch marks, raised blood pressure and blood sugar, and suppressed natural steroids.[2] Dermatology literature groups it with mercury and hydroquinone among the most toxic and widely used lightening agents.[2]

A 2019 cross-sectional survey of 262 female health science students in Borama, Somaliland found that 25.6 percent had ever used lightening products. Of 56 products the authors bought locally, 22 listed a corticosteroid and 12 of those contained clobetasol; more than 60 percent of users did not know their product's active ingredients. Only 9 percent reported no side effects, with skin atrophy, acne and allergic contact dermatitis most common, and users were more likely than non-users to believe lighter skin brings confidence, job and marriage prospects.[9]

A 2012 letter in the Medical Journal of Australia describes a 24-year-old woman who used three creams containing hydroquinone, clobetasol propionate 0.05 percent and betamethasone 0.05 percent for a prolonged period and presented with fatigue, facial oedema, Cushingoid features and suppressed cortisol; she was treated with short-term glucocorticoid replacement, and pigmentation returned about four weeks after stopping the creams. The authors noted that internet sales bypass prescribing controls and that ingredients may not be disclosed.[10]

Wikipedia's skin-whitening article places the practice in a wider context: over 25 percent of women in Africa and around 40 percent in Asia are reported to use lightening products, with motivations tied to beauty ideals, social mobility, marriage and employment, and also to concealing pimples, rashes or vitiligo. It lists corticosteroids such as clobetasol among the commonest agents, alongside mercury and hydroquinone.[16]

subs.h: Use in training and appearance forums
paras: On T Nation, clobetasol appears in a 2011 thread where a user prescribed a topical steroid for hair loss on a forearm asked what it might do to testosterone levels.[17] Discussion of the drug in looksmaxxing forums is otherwise sparse; it appears mainly in skincare and skin-lightening contexts.

Clobetasol is prescription-only in the United States, and non-prescription sale is illegal there, although some countries sell it without a prescription.[2] The Somaliland survey found no regulation of lightening products and over-the-counter sales in shops, pharmacies and supermarkets; it cited a 2014 Nairobi workshop recommending restrictions on hydroquinone, mercury and corticosteroid-containing products.[9] The EU banned hydroquinone from cosmetics in 2000.[16]

lore.intro: Clobetasol is discussed in appearance communities mostly in connection with skin lightening and steroid-related skin harms, with little forum material on its prescribed use.[9][11][17]
